planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost; Lassen is a female cultivar released by UC Davis as a Kerman alternative and still needs a male pollinator such as Peters or Randy planted nearby for wind pollination.

directions: Lassen was released by the University of California, Davis pistachio breeding program as an alternative female cultivar to the industry-standard Kerman, bred to bear more precociously and produce a more consistent annual crop rather than Kerman's pronounced alternate-year bearing pattern. It requires the same demanding climate as any pistachio: hot, dry, low-humidity summers paired with sufficient winter chill to break dormancy uniformly, and it performs poorly in humid or marine climates even where cold hours are adequate. Plant in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil and pair with a male pollinizer that sheds pollen at the same time, since pistachios are entirely dioecious and wind-pollinated. Harvest in early autumn once the hulls loosen and the characteristic shell split appears; trees need roughly seven to ten years to reach significant production.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension -- Pistachio Production Manual
UC Davis Fruit & Nut Research and Information Center

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Ikaika is a Hawaii Agriculture Experiment Station selection (HAES 333) valued for its sturdy, wind-resistant growth habit and is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Ikaika (HAES 333) is a Hawaii-developed macadamia selection prized in commercial orchards for its unusually strong, compact branching structure, which holds up well to the strong trade winds common on Hawaii's macadamia-growing slopes where more brittle cultivars suffer limb breakage. It bears a reliable, moderate crop of good cracking-quality nuts on a vigorous tree and is often planted as a windbreak selection within mixed orchard blocks alongside higher-yielding cultivars. Like other macadamias it needs many years of warm, frost-free growth before significant bearing, along with a compatible cross-pollinator. Water regularly during nut development and allow nuts to fall naturally before harvest.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources (CTAHR)

planting.note: Plant seeds in fall for natural stratification or plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline, dry, rocky soil in full sun; native to the arid pinyon-juniper belt of southern California's peninsular ranges and northern Baja California.

directions: Plant in dry, rocky, very well-drained soil in full sun, mimicking the arid desert-mountain slopes of the southern California and Baja California peninsular ranges where this species naturally occurs. Parry pinyon is unusual among pinyons for bearing needles in bundles of four rather than the more typical one or two, giving rise to its alternate name of four-leaf pinyon, and it forms a slow-growing, rounded small tree well adapted to poor, thin desert soils. It produces large, wingless, edible seeds similar in size and quality to other pinyon pines and has long been harvested by Indigenous peoples of the Colorado Desert region. Extremely drought tolerant once established and essentially intolerant of summer irrigation or heavy soils.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in humus-rich, acidic, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; best suited to mild, humid, marine climates such as the Pacific Northwest coast rather than hot, dry, or hard-freezing regions.

directions: Native to the temperate rainforests of Chile and adjacent Argentina, this evergreen Proteaceae relative of macadamia produces clusters of small, round, orange-red nuts with a mild flavor often compared to a cross between hazelnut and macadamia, prized locally for pressing into a light culinary oil as well as for out-of-hand eating. It prefers cool, humid, mild-winter climates with consistent moisture and acidic, well-drained soil, performing best in Pacific coastal regions and struggling in areas with intense summer heat, drought, or hard freezes below the mid-teens Fahrenheit. Plant in filtered sun to partial shade in warmer climates to protect foliage from scorch, and expect several years of establishment before the tree begins bearing its distinctive fern-like, glossy compound leaves and drooping nut clusters.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew -- Plants of the World Online
